claims.text: Near-optimal, modest-magnitude inter-elemental mixing enthalpy governs structural and chemical stability in near-equiatomic high-entropy nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy counteracts segregation and intermetallic formation in these nanoparticles.
The relevant initial material is a nanoparticle containing at least five metals in equal or near-equal ratios and crystallized as a single-phase solid solution.
Small composition changes that preserve near-equiatomic ratios can systematically alter the overall mixing enthalpy.
Thermal cycling over 473–1923 K can test the effect of mixing enthalpy under catalytic or thermoelectric operating conditions.
A balance between modest mixing enthalpy and configurational entropy stabilizes a single-phase structure.
This thermodynamic balance prevents phase separation and intermetallic-compound formation.
When mixing enthalpy is neither too exothermic nor too endothermic, configurational entropy dominates at elevated temperature.
Entropy dominance at elevated temperature stabilizes a homogeneous solid solution.
Deviations from the proposed enthalpy balance create a driving force for nucleation of secondary phases or chemical segregation.
Nanoparticles designed with optimal mixing enthalpy will retain a single-phase, homogeneously mixed state across 473–1923 K.
Optimally mixed nanoparticles will show minimal segregation or intermetallic formation.
Retention of the homogeneous single phase will preserve catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Samples with deliberately non-optimal mixing enthalpy will exhibit more phase separation or chemical change than optimized samples.
Samples with deliberately non-optimal mixing enthalpy will suffer diminished catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Rapid diffusion can override equilibrium thermodynamic stabilization.
Aggressive oxidation or other extreme reactive conditions can introduce degradation pathways not captured by the proposed thermodynamic mechanism.
XRD, TEM-EDS, XPS, and performance measurements can compare phase purity, elemental homogeneity, chemical state, and functional retention between optimized and perturbed samples.
The hypothesis is falsified if optimized samples show similar or greater segregation, decomposition, or performance loss than deliberately perturbed samples under the same conditions.

contradictions.description: The conditions seek hold times that allow equilibrium to be approached, whereas the boundary states that rapid diffusion can override equilibrium thermodynamic stabilization. Rapid diffusion ordinarily promotes equilibration rather than overriding equilibrium, so the role of kinetics is described inconsistently.

The intervention calls for only slight changes in mixing enthalpy, while the falsification design calls for substantially more negative or positive mixing enthalpy. The intended perturbation magnitude is therefore inconsistent.
